title: Finite-state automata for exact matrix product operators of tight-binding Hamiltonians: fractals, quasicrystals, trees and hyperbolic lattices
authors: Marta Brzezińska, Jeanne Colbois, Loïc Herviou
abstract: Inspired by the recent progress in the simulation of tight-binding Hamiltonians on large lattices using tensor networks, we introduce a systematic matrix product operator (MPO) construction for single-particle Hamiltonians on recursively structured lattices. Taking advantage of this recursive structure, we encode the lattice geometry in a finite-state automaton and, adapting ideas from Abelian-symmetric tensor networks, obtain an exact and analytical MPO representation of the Hamiltonian, where the number of tensors grows logarithmically with the system size and the bond dimension is set by the number of automaton states. Several examples demonstrate the generality of the framework: regular lattices, fractals, Cayley trees, hyperbolic lattices, and one- and two-dimensional Fibonacci quasicrystals. Combined with the kernel polynomial method, these MPO representations enable large-scale calculations of spectral properties without explicitly constructing the full Hamiltonian. This provides a unified route to the exploration of electronic properties across a broad class of lattices at exponentially large system sizes.
summary: This paper introduces a novel method to exactly represent the Hamiltonian of tight-binding models on complex lattices (like fractals and hyperbolic spaces) as a Matrix Product Operator (MPO). By encoding the lattice geometry using a finite-state automaton, the method ensures the computational cost scales only logarithmically with system size. This allows for large-scale, analytical calculations of electronic properties across a vast range of structured materials.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a systematic, exact, and analytical method to represent the Matrix Product Operator (MPO) for single-particle Hamiltonians on complex, recursively structured lattices.
main_result: They achieve this by encoding the lattice geometry within a finite-state automaton, resulting in an MPO whose bond dimension grows only logarithmically with system size.
method: The core method combines finite-state automata to encode lattice structure with tensor network techniques (MPO) and utilizes the Kernel Polynomial Method (KPM) for spectral calculations.
model_or_system: The model is the tight-binding Hamiltonian, applied to a broad class of lattices including regular Bravais lattices, fractals (e.g., Sierpinski Carpet), quasiperiodic chains (e.g., Fibonacci), Cayley trees, and hyperbolic lattices.
key_observables: Spectral properties, Density of States (DOS), and Local Density of States (LDOS).
important_parameters: The bond dimension ($\chi$), which is determined by the number of automaton states and remains finite for these structured lattices.
main_assumptions: The framework critically relies on the recursive structure of the lattices to ensure the automaton state space, and thus the bond dimension, remains finite and manageable.
figures_summary: Figure 6 illustrates the evolution of the MPO bond dimensions versus the number of iterations for various lattice types, showing differences in growth rates.
paper_structure: The paper is structured to first introduce the general formalism (Section II), followed by detailed constructions for specific lattice types: regular, fractal, quasiperiodic, and hyperbolic lattices.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general computational framework for simulating electronic structure on geometrically complex systems that are difficult for standard methods, bridging geometry and tensor network efficiency.
